claims.text: Public and private sectors classify activity by ownership and control. A public-sector enterprise is owned and controlled by the state, whereas private-sector activity is owned and controlled by private individuals or organisations. A government-owned bus operator and an individually owned bus operator can provide the same service while belonging to different ownership sectors. Their activity does not settle their ownership. A mixed economy combines public and private activity. Public provision can pursue access to essential services or employment as well as financial sustainability. Private owners commonly seek profit and business survival, although a private organisation may also pursue social aims. Neither label proves that the organisation is efficient or that every service is free. Public enterprises may charge customers and private providers may supply services under government contracts. Organising privately can involve a sole trader, partnership or company; public activity can be organised through government departments or state-owned enterprises. Ownership forms are developed in topic 2.1. A company described as public limited has shares available to the public; that name does not by itself make it state owned. Ask who owns and controls it before assigning its ownership sector.

claims.text: Nationalisation transfers a privately owned business or industry into state ownership and control. Privatisation transfers a state-owned business or activity into private ownership and control. The directions are opposite: private to state, or state to private. A new owner may change objectives, investment and decisions, but a change in owner is distinct from a guaranteed improvement in performance. Nationalisation may protect essential service access but creates state financing demands. Privatisation may introduce commercial incentives, but service conditions may be needed to protect unprofitable users. A sale to investors within Namibia is still privatisation if state ownership transfers to private owners. Nationalisation does not mean selling abroad or banning imports; those concern international trade, not a transfer of ownership. Identify the enterprise whose ownership changes.

claims.text: Assume a fictional state-owned coach company is sold entirely to private investors. In a separate event the state buys a privately owned water supplier. The coach sale is privatisation because ownership moves from state to private investors. The water purchase is nationalisation because it moves in the reverse direction. The buyers’ nationality does not determine either classification.

claims.text: Activity sectors classify what is done. Primary businesses obtain natural resources; secondary businesses transform materials into products or carry out construction; tertiary businesses supply services. Follow the activity rather than the owner or product’s final user. Growing mahangu is primary, milling it into flour is secondary, and transporting or selling the flour is tertiary. Transport does not physically manufacture the flour even though it adds value by making it available where needed. A business can operate in more than one activity sector. An enterprise growing fruit, making juice and running its own shop has primary, secondary and tertiary operations. If asked to classify one operation, classify that operation. If describing the whole enterprise, explain its combination rather than assuming a single label covers every stage. Public/private ownership is a separate axis: a privately owned farm is both private sector and primary sector. Development of services does not remove the economy’s need for materials or manufactured goods; the sectors supply inputs and customers to one another.

claims.text: Osha Clay extracts clay near Otjiwarongo, Imba Pots shapes and fires it, and Hela Couriers delivers the pots to buyers. Classifying the process avoids confusing a customer’s ownership with a supplier’s activity.

claims.text: Business size can be described through legal form of ownership, nature of business, nature of product, capital employed, total assets, number of employees, level of technology, market share, turnover, profitability and value of output. Two straightforward numerical measures are the number of employees and annual turnover. No single indicator ranks every business fairly. A highly automated producer may employ fewer people than a labour-intensive workshop but produce much more. Some indicators are descriptive clues, such as ownership form or technology, rather than a numerical scale. Others measure different things: turnover is sales revenue, profit is the surplus after costs, and total assets is the value of resources owned. Select a measure suited to the comparison and state the time period or valuation basis. Compare similar activities where possible and use several indicators if they disagree. Large does not necessarily mean successful, profitable or well managed. A small specialist may earn a high profit relative to its investment, while a large producer can make a loss.

claims.text: Classification groups businesses by a shared characteristic, such as activity sector or ownership. Measurement indicates scale through an appropriate size indicator. Governments can use sector and employment information to identify where support or infrastructure may be needed. A lender can compare an applicant with businesses of similar activity and scale instead of interpreting its turnover without context. Managers can monitor changes over time and compare competitors. Investors may use size data as background, but size alone cannot establish return or safety. A classification is useful only if its categories fit the question. Primary/secondary/tertiary helps describe economic activity; public/private helps describe ownership. Neither directly ranks business size. Measurement must also be consistent: compare annual turnover over the same length of time and avoid comparing one firm’s sales revenue with another’s profit. Two businesses may be similar in employment but different in assets, so describe that result instead of forcing a single ranking. The purpose of the decision determines the most useful classification and measure.

claims.text: A local planning office needs to assess employment opportunities in food processing. It receives employment totals for food factories and sales totals for farms. Farm turnover cannot be treated as the missing factory employee count.

claims.text: Small firms can survive by meeting needs that large suppliers cannot serve profitably or flexibly. A narrow local market may support a small repairer but not a large branch. Personal service can help an owner learn customer preferences, adjust an order quickly and win repeat business. A specialist may make customised goods that do not suit a standard production line. Close contact between owner, workers and customers can shorten decisions. Low overhead commitments may also help, although a small firm does not automatically have a lower cost per unit. Large rivals may obtain purchasing advantages if orders are sufficiently large and coordination remains effective. Small firms face disadvantages such as limited finance, dependence on a few customers and the owner’s limited time. Survival therefore requires enough demand and revenue to cover costs, not merely being friendly. Some owners deliberately remain small to preserve control and a manageable workload. Others are newly established businesses that may later grow. Judge survival against the actual customers and resources: a niche can protect a small supplier, but losing a major customer can make that niche too narrow.
